study.title: Ezekiel 34 O Lord against the evil shepherds and for his flock
study.overview: This chapter counters two ways of leading the people: the human shepherds who feed on the sheep and leave them scattered, and the Lord himself, who promises to seek, bring back, heal, guard, and feed his flock. The first part denounces leaders who fail to care for the weak, the wounded and the dispersed, ruling hard and seeking self-interest. Then God announces judgment against these shepherds and personally assumes the task of rescuing the scattered sheep. Then the text extends the promise: the Lord makes a distinction between sheep and sheep, judges the strong who oppress the weak and raises a single shepherd to feed the people. The conclusion seals hope with a pact of peace, security, provision and recognition that the Lord is with his people.

outline.title: Accusation against the shepherds of Israel
outline.explanation: The word of the Lord denounces leaders who serve themselves as the flock instead of caring for him. They fail to strengthen, heal, seek and bring back the sheep, and therefore the people spread and are exposed to danger.

outline.title: God stands against the unfaithful shepherds
outline.explanation: The Lord declares that he will demand his sheep from the hands of the evil shepherds and prevent them from continuing to exploit the flock. The care of the people will no longer be handed over to abusive leaders.

outline.title: The Lord Himself will seek and restore the flock
outline.explanation: God promises to act as a true shepherd: to seek the scattered, to gather the scattered, to bring them back to the earth, to feed them in good pastures and to treat them with justice, healing the weak and wounded.

outline.title: Judgment between the sheep, one shepherd and the peace covenant
outline.explanation: The Lord also judges the sheep against each other, denouncing the strong that harm the weak. Then he promises to raise a Davidic pastor, make a covenant of peace, grant security, rain, fruit and abundance, and conclude that the flock is human and belongs to his pasture under the rule of God Himself.

study.context: The notes provided understand the "pastors" as the leaders of Israel, including rulers and, in some readings, priests and responsible for the public conduct of the people. The chapter is presented as part of a larger sequence in which the Lord announces restoration after judgment, with pastoral image to describe government, care and reintegration of the people.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that leadership, from God's perspective, exists to serve, protect and restore, not to explore. The divine judgment lies both unfaithful leaders and members of the people who oppress the weak. At the same time, hope rests on God to assume the role of a pastor, gathering his people, and in a Davidic pastor who rules as an instrument of the Lord Himself. The language of peace covenant shows that restoration includes renewed communion with God, community security and concrete blessing in the life of the people. The final statement that the sheep are human and God is their God highlights a relationship of belonging, care, and holy authority.

scholarViews.insight: The scattered and unleashed sheep show the result of the neglect and abuse of the leaders; God promises to seek them and bring them back.
The text treats Israel's pastors as responsible for their neglect and shows God demanding of them account for the damage caused to the flock.
The image of the flock points to people, that of the pasture to the church, and that of the pastor to the Messiah through whom God is the God of his people.

questions: What forms of leadership today seem more like the pastoring that the text condemns, and how does it appear in practice?
In which areas do you feel more like a wounded, dispersed or weakened sheep, and how does God's care respond to it?
How does the promise of one pastor and a peace pact correct rivalries, abuses and inequalities within God's people?
study.practice: Examine your way of exerting influence, even on a small scale: at home, in the church, at work or among friends. The text calls leadership to strengthen the weak, seek the absent and avoid the use of people for their own benefit. This week, practice concrete care with someone vulnerable: listen without haste, help restore a relationship, visit who is away or share resources with whom you need. At the same time, rest on the promise that God even seeks his people and does not abandon the lost sheep.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the denunciation to the leaders of Israel, the promise of restoration, the reading of the Davidic pastor as a Messianic figure and the spiritual meaning of the flock. However, it is not possible to detail with certainty, from only these notes, all internal historical references or closedly define the exact extent of each symbol in each verse. Some confessional readings present in the commentators are interpretations, not mandatory conclusions of the text.
